sections.normalized_html:
Recall that a linear Diophantine equation [MATH: ax+by=c] has a solution if and only if [MATH: d \: | \: c,] where [MATH: d = \text{gcd}(a,b).]

With that in mind, let's examine each equation in turn.

  • Equation I has solutions. We have [MATH: a=18,] [MATH: b=15,] and [MATH: c=24.] Since [MATH: d=\text{gcd}(18,15)=3] and [MATH: 3 \: | \: 24,] our equation has solutions.

  • Equation II has no solution. We have [MATH: a=7,] [MATH: b=-28,] and [MATH: c=10.] Since [MATH: d=\text{gcd}(7,-28)=7] and [MATH: 7 \!\not{|}\: 10,] our equation has no solution.

  • Equation III has no solution. We have [MATH: a=9,] [MATH: b=27,] and [MATH: c=16.] Since [MATH: d=\text{gcd}(9,27)=9] and [MATH: 9 \!\not{|}\: 16,] our equation has no solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: (x,y)=(15,14)] is a solution of the Diophantine equation [MATH: 11x-13y=-17,] and that [MATH: (\overset{\sim}{x},\overset{\sim}{y})] is the solution with the smallest possible positive value of [MATH: x,] what is the value of [MATH: \overset{\sim}{x}?]
sections.readable_text: Given that [MATH: (x,y)=(15,14)] is a solution of the Diophantine equation [MATH: 11x-13y=-17,] and that [MATH: (\overset{\sim}{x},\overset{\sim}{y})] is the solution with the smallest possible positive value of [MATH: x,] what is the value of [MATH: \overset{\sim}{x}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, recall that a linear Diophantine equation [MATH: ax+by=c] has a solution if and only if [MATH: d \: | \: c,] where [MATH: d = \text{gcd}(a,b).] Moreover, if [MATH: (x_0,y_0)] is a solution to the equation, then the general solution is given by [MATH: \left(x_0+\dfrac{b}{d}t, \, y_0-\dfrac{a}{d}t\right), \qquad t=0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots]

Here, we have [MATH: a=11,] [MATH: b=-13,] [MATH: c=-17,] and

[MATH: d=\text{gcd}(11,-13)=1.]

Since [MATH: (15,14)] is a solution of [MATH: 11x-13y=-17,] the general solution must be

[MATH: \left(15+\dfrac{(-13)}{1}t, \, 14-\dfrac{11}{1}t\right) = (15-13t, \, 14-11t),]

where [MATH: t=0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots \, .]

The smallest possible positive value of [MATH: x=15-13t] is attained when [MATH: t=1.] Therefore,

[MATH: \overset{\sim}{x} = 15-13 \cdot 1 = 2.]

We have the linear Diophantine equation

[MATH: ax+by=c] where [MATH: a=2,] [MATH: b=7,] and [MATH: c=10.] We're given that the equation has solutions.

Notice that our equation can't be solved for either of the two variables using integer coefficients. So, let's find the linear representation of [MATH: \text{gcd}(2,7)] using the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

[MATH: 7|=|2 ⋅ 3|+|1; ↙|↙; 2|=|1 ⋅ 2|+|0]

Solving for the remainders (the rightmost terms) in the equations above, we get

[MATH: 1|= 7 − 2 ⋅ 3.]

As a result, we obtain that [MATH: d=\text{gcd}(a,b) = 1] and

[MATH: 2 \cdot (-3) + 7 = 1.]

Multiplying this equation by [MATH: 10,] we get

[MATH: 2 ⋅ (− 3) + 7|= 1; 2 ⋅ (− 3) ⋅ 10 + 7 ⋅ 10|= 10; 2 ⋅ (− 30) + 7 ⋅ 10|= 10,]

which means that [MATH: (x,y)=(-30,10)] is a solution to our Diophantine equation.

Now, the general solution is

[MATH: \left(-30+\dfrac{b}{d}t, \, 10-\dfrac{a}{d}t\right) = (-30+7t, \, 10-2t),]

where [MATH: t=0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots \,.]

The smallest possible positive value of [MATH: x=-30+7t] is attained when [MATH: t=5.] Therefore,

[MATH: \overset{\sim}{x} = -30+7 \cdot 5 = 5.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A linear Diophantine equation with two variables [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] takes the form

Content:
[MATH: ax+by=c,]

Content:
where [MATH: a,] [MATH: b,] and [MATH: c] are integer constants. A solution of a Diophantine equation is any integer pair [MATH: (x,y)] that satisfies the equation.

Content:
For example, the Diophantine equation

Content:
[MATH: 2x+3y=9]

Content:
has an infinite number of integer solutions:

Content:
[MATH: (3, 1), \quad (6, -1), \quad (15, -7), \quad \ldots]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying a Solution of a Linear Diophantine Equation

Example Prompt:
Which of the following pairs [MATH: (x,y)] are solutions of the Diophantine equation [MATH: 3x+8y=5?]

1. [MATH: (7,-2)]
2. [MATH: (22,-8)]
3. [MATH: (15,-5)]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's check each pair in turn.

- [MATH: (7,-2)] is a solution of our equation. Indeed, substituting [MATH: x=7] and [MATH: y=-2,] we obtain
[MATH: 3x + 8y|= 5; 3 ⋅ 7 + 8 ⋅ (− 2)|= 5; 21 − 16|= 5; 5|= 5✓]
- [MATH: (22,-8)] is not a solution of our equation. Substituting [MATH: x=22] and [MATH: y=-8,] we obtain
[MATH: 3x + 8y|= 5; 3 ⋅ 22 + 8 ⋅ (− 8)|= 5; 66 − 64|= 5; 2|≠ 5×]
- [MATH: (15,-5)] is a solution of our equation. Indeed, substituting [MATH: x=15] and [MATH: y=-5,] we obtain
[MATH: 3x + 8y|= 5; 3 ⋅ 15 + 8 ⋅ (− 5)|= 5; 45 − 40|= 5; 5|= 5✓]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: When a Linear Diophantine Equation Has No Solutions

Content:
The linear Diophantine equation

Content:
[MATH: ax+by=c]

Content:
has a solution if and only if [MATH: d \: | \: c,] where [MATH: d = \text{gcd}(a,b).]

Content:
Let's use the theorem to test some Diophantine equations.

Content:
- Consider the equation
[MATH: 2x+10y=17.]
Here, we have [MATH: a=2,] [MATH: b=10,] and [MATH: c=17.] Notice that
[MATH: d=\text{gcd}(2,10)=2]
and [MATH: 2 \!\not{|}\: 17.] Therefore, according to the theorem, our equation has no solution.

Content:
Indeed, notice that the expression on the left-hand side ([MATH: 2x+10y]) is always an even number, while the right-hand side of the equation ([MATH: 17]) is an odd number. As a result, there is no solution.

Content:
- Consider the equation
[MATH: 4x+5y=7.]
Here, we have [MATH: a=4,] [MATH: b=5,] and [MATH: c=7.] Since
[MATH: d=\text{gcd}(4,5)=1]
and [MATH: 1 \:{|}\: 7,] our equation has solutions.

Content:
Indeed, one of the solutions for [MATH: 4x+5y=7] is the pair [MATH: (3,-1).]

---

Item 6 — Example: Identifying Whether a Linear Diophantine Equation Has a Solution

Example Prompt:
Which of the following Diophantine equations have solutions?

1. [MATH: 18x+15y=24]
2. [MATH: 7x-28y=10]
3. [MATH: 9x+27y=16]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that a linear Diophantine equation
[MATH: ax+by=c]
has a solution if and only if [MATH: d \: | \: c,] where [MATH: d = \text{gcd}(a,b).]

With that in mind, let's examine each equation in turn.

- Equation I has solutions. We have [MATH: a=18,] [MATH: b=15,] and [MATH: c=24.] Since
[MATH: d=\text{gcd}(18,15)=3]
and [MATH: 3 \: | \: 24,] our equation has solutions.
- Equation II has no solution. We have [MATH: a=7,] [MATH: b=-28,] and [MATH: c=10.] Since
[MATH: d=\text{gcd}(7,-28)=7]
and [MATH: 7 \!\not{|}\: 10,] our equation has no solution.
- Equation III has no solution. We have [MATH: a=9,] [MATH: b=27,] and [MATH: c=16.] Since
[MATH: d=\text{gcd}(9,27)=9]
and [MATH: 9 \!\not{|}\: 16,] our equation has no solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

---

Item 9 — Tutorial: The General Solution of a Linear Diophantine Equation

Content:
If [MATH: (x_0,y_0)] is any particular solution of the equation, then the set of all solutions consists of integer pairs

Content:
[MATH: \left( x_0 + \dfrac{b}{d}t, \: y_0 - \dfrac{a}{d}t \right), \qquad t = 0, \pm 1, \pm2, \ldots \: .]

Content:
In particular, if [MATH: d=1,] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \left( x_0 + bt, \: y_0 - at \right), \qquad t = 0, \pm 1, \pm2, \ldots \: .]

Content:
For example, given that [MATH: (x,y)=(4,-1)] is a solution of the Diophantine equation

Content:
[MATH: 4x+5y=11,]

Content:
find its general solution.

Content:
Here, we have [MATH: a=4,] [MATH: b=5,] and [MATH: c=11.] Since [MATH: (4,-1)] is a solution of [MATH: 4x+5y=11,] the general solution must be

Content:
[MATH: (4 + (5)/(1)t, − 1 − (4)/(1)t)|= (4 + 5t, − 1 − 4t),]

Content:
where [MATH: t=0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots \, .]

---

Item 10 — Example: Finding the General Solution of a Linear Diophantine Equation Given One of Its Solutions

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: (x,y)=(15,14)] is a solution of the Diophantine equation [MATH: 11x-13y=-17,] and that [MATH: (\overset{\sim}{x},\overset{\sim}{y})] is the solution with the smallest possible positive value of [MATH: x,] what is the value of [MATH: \overset{\sim}{x}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, recall that a linear Diophantine equation
[MATH: ax+by=c]
has a solution if and only if [MATH: d \: | \: c,] where [MATH: d = \text{gcd}(a,b).] Moreover, if [MATH: (x_0,y_0)] is a solution to the equation, then the general solution is given by
[MATH: \left(x_0+\dfrac{b}{d}t, \, y_0-\dfrac{a}{d}t\right), \qquad t=0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots]

Here, we have [MATH: a=11,] [MATH: b=-13,] [MATH: c=-17,] and

[MATH: d=\text{gcd}(11,-13)=1.]

Since [MATH: (15,14)] is a solution of [MATH: 11x-13y=-17,] the general solution must be

[MATH: \left(15+\dfrac{(-13)}{1}t, \, 14-\dfrac{11}{1}t\right) = (15-13t, \, 14-11t),]

where [MATH: t=0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots \, .]

The smallest possible positive value of [MATH: x=15-13t] is attained when [MATH: t=1.] Therefore,

[MATH: \overset{\sim}{x} = 15-13 \cdot 1 = 2.]

---
